# Introduction

With the advance of the times and the development of information technology, the classroom teaching forms of technology integration are more and more diverse (Mueller et al., 2008), which puts forward higher requirements for teachers’ digital literacy, especially digital teaching compe- tence (Liu et al., 2017). In the newly released _Reimagining our futures together: In a new social contract for education_, UNESCO proposed to expand the time and space of education, strengthen digital infrastructure, manage digital learning spaces, and use digital technologies to support public and inclusive education for a shared future (UNESCO, 2021). According to data released by UNESCO, more than 1.5 billion teachers and students worldwide were aAected by the COVID-19 pandemic. The epidemic had triggered the demand for online education for teachers, forcing the digital transformation of education and the development of digital literacy for teachers (Sánchez-Cruzado et al., 2021). However, according to the UNESCO study, teachers have not yet been able to realize the advantages and potential of innovative education models based on information technology. Teachers in developing countries, in particular, face the dilemma of inadequate information

technology infrastructure and high-quality online resources, and lack the resources and capacity to develop their digital literacy (UNESCO, 2022). The _Teacher Digital Literacy_ issued by the Chinese Ministry of Education in 2022 clearly stated that teachers should enhance their awareness, ability and responsibility to utilize digital technologies to optimize, innovate and transform educational activ- ities (MOE, 2022). In general, digital technologies are products or services supported by information technologies, including digital artefacts, digital platforms, digital infrastructure, and so on (Saeed & Sidorova, 2023). They are tools for digital transformation and are the core of digital infrastructure, digital platforms and digital innovation. The digital technology in this study refers to the general teaching software used by teachers (e.g., PowerPoint), subject-speciflc teaching software (e.g., the Geometer’s Sketchpad, GeoGebra), various online education resources (e.g., learning websites and online courses), and various digital teaching devices (e.g., interactive whiteboard) (MOE, 2022). The evolution of digital teaching practices can be traced back to 2001, marking the inception of the application of information technology in mathematics education (Borba et al., [2016)](#orcid). With the rapid development of modern information technology, the space-time of learning and the bound- aries of education have been greatly expanded, giving birth to new forms of digital education (Duncheon & Tierney, 2013). This process can be divided into four stages: traditional classroom teaching environment, simple multimedia learning environment, interactive multimedia learning environment, and intelligent learning environment (Nan & Zhang, 2019). Since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, the development of digital education has further accelerated (Cone et al., 2022). At present, information technology and education are integrating and developing, continu- ously promoting educational reform and innovation. For example, in 2013, UK began exploring the enhancement of teaching quality and optimization of educational management through digital means. The Singapore government launched a national digital literacy training programme to improve students’ digital capabilities by improving hardware, software facilities, and curriculum settings (Kong et al., 2014). The Italian government has connected high-speed broadband to 32,000 primary and secondary schools nationwide. In this process, we gradually see the trend of diversiflca- tion and intelligent development in education (Roll & Wylie, 2016).

Mathematics is a very important subject for elementary school students, which is the basis of many other disciplines. Mathematics teacher’s digital teaching behaviour is very critical to improve students’ mathematics learning eAects (Viberg et al., 2020). Empirical studies suggest that digital tools can signiflcantly enhance student engagement and motivation by oAering interactive and personalized learning experiences (Borba et al., [2016)](#orcid). The use of technology supports collaborative learning, fostering essential skills such as teamwork and communication. Additionally, digital plat- forms provide access to a vast array of educational resources, facilitating deeper exploration of subjects and broadening students’ perspectives (Nan & Zhang, 2019). Moreover, technology has been shown to improve academic performance, particularly in STEM flelds, by promoting higher- order thinking skills through project-based and inquiry-based learning. The immediate feedback provided by digital tools also contributes to more eAective learning by allowing students to quickly understand and correct their mistakes (Cone et al., 2022). Overall, the strategic use of digital technology in education holds the potential to transform learning experiences and outcomes for the better. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the current situation of elementary school mathematics teachers’ adoption of digital technology for teaching, and to explore the main factors that aAect their digital teaching behaviour.

Previous studies analysed the eAects of subject-speciflc digital technologies such as dynamic mathematics software on mathematics teaching and learning and elementary school mathematics teachers’ usage behaviour of speciflc digital technologies (Birgin & Acar, [2020;](#orcid) Yuan, et al., 2023b; Zengin et al., 2012). There are also some studies indicating that teachers’ utilization of digital tools has become a strategic pillar for high-quality of education worldwide (Avvisati et al., [2013)](#orcid). A study from Stockholm University, for example, highlighted that teachers expect institutions to play a signiflcant role in digital education by helping them address challenges, deflne the role of institu- tions in digital education (Lindfors et al., 2021). The “Using Data Project” funded by the National 

ASIA PACIFIC JOURNAL OF EDUCATION 3

Science Foundation in the USA also aims to help educators develop data literacy (Shim & Yoon,  2024). It involves teachers in rigorous data analysis and re’ective conversations to improve teaching and learning in mathematics education. In addition, the cultural background of a country or region can signiflcantly in’uence the adoption and integration of digital tools in mathematics education (Li et al., 2023). For instance, collectivist cultures, which emphasize group harmony and interdepen- dence, may encourage collaborative and interactive digital learning environments (Hornik & Tupchiy, 2006). In contrast, individualistic cultures might focus more on self-paced and personalized digital learning tools (Hornik & Tupchiy, 2006). Rules also play a crucial role in shaping the use of digital tools by mathematics teachers (Hoyles, 2018). They can either facilitate or hinder the integration of technology in the classroom by providing resources, training, and support or by imposing restrictive regulations (Beldarrain, [2006)](#orcid).

Based on previous studies, several factors signiflcantly in’uence the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers. Teacher education plays a pivotal role, often surpassing the mere access to technological tools (Yuan et al., 2023b). The level of data literacy and under- standing of technology ethics are emerging as critical factors shaping pre-service teachers’ digital teaching competence (Li et al., 2023). Furthermore, the innovative behaviour of these teachers is in’uenced by the support and resources provided by their educational institutions, which can either foster or hinder the integration of digital technologies into their teaching practices (Lindfors et al.,  2021). Additionally, the educational level of teachers, with a higher percentage having an under- graduate degree, has been linked to a greater propensity for digital technology adoption in the classroom (Birgin & Acar, [2020)](#orcid). These factors underscore the importance of comprehensive teacher training, institutional support, and the recognition of the evolving role of technology in education. However, limited research had explored other factors in’uencing the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers. In order to flnd out the main in’uential factors of mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour, this study tried to answer the following two research questions:

1. What factors positively aAect the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathe- matics teachers based on the UTAUT-TPACK model?
2. Which one is the biggest in’uential factor aAecting digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers based on the UTAUT-TPACK model?

# Literature review and hypothesis development

## _Digital technology and elementary school mathematics teaching_

Digital transformation is profoundly aAecting all sectors of society (Mueller et al., 2008; Skare et al.,  2023; Vial, 2021). Digital technology is the tool of digital transformation and the core of digital infrastructure, digital platforms and digital innovation (Saeed & Sidorova, 2023). Digital technology is now widely used in various disciplines (Antonietti et al., [2022;](#orcid) Collins & Halverson, 2010; Sailer et al.,  2021; Scherer et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2016). In order to successfully complete teaching tasks and achieve better teaching results, teachers need to know their teaching environ- ment well, have suficient knowledge about digital technology, and be able to use this knowledge properly in teaching (Gomez-Trigueros, 2023). Mathematics is a core subject, and mathematics learning is very necessary for the learning of other related subjects and the future career develop-

## _UTAUT and Digital teaching_

Davis proposed the flrst-generation technology acceptance model (TAM) in 1989 (Davis et al., 1989). This model proposed two main cognitive beliefs that aAect users’ technology acceptance: perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Venkatesh and Davis proposed the second-generation technology acceptance model (TAM2) in 2000, which explored the in’uence of social and cognitive processes on the perceived usefulness, behavioural intention and usage behaviour of speciflc technologies (Venkatesh & Davis, 2000). In 2003, Venkatesh et al. formally proposed a unifled theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) on the basis of integration of technology acceptance theory, theory of planned behaviour, diAusion of innovation theory, social cognitive theory and other flelds (Venkatesh et al., 2003). The model proposed four main factors that in’uence users’ acceptance and use of technology: performance expectancy (PE), eAort expectancy (EE), social in’uence (SI), and facilitating conditions (FC), and four moderating factors involving individual diAerences: gender, age, experience, and voluntariness of use. Performance expectancy refers to the degree to which users believe that using the system will help them improve their work performance. EAort expectancy refers to the degree to which users think the system is easy to use. Social in’uence refers to the degree to which users perceive that people around them expect them to use the system. Facilitating conditions refers to the extent to which users believe that an organized, skilled infrastructure and resources exist to support their use of the system. According to the UTAUT model (Venkatesh et al., 2003), performance expectancy, eAort expectancy and social in’uence directly aAect users’ behavioural intention; facilitating conditions directly aAect usage behaviour, and users’ behavioural intention directly aAect usage behaviour. The UTAUT model is widely used because its explanatory power of user behaviour is nearly 70%, which is far higher than other technology acceptance models (Al-Nuaimi & Al-Emran, [2021;](#orcid) Alghazi et al., [2020;](#orcid) Aytekin et al., [ 2022;](#orcid) Grani(, 2022; Qiao et al., 2021; Shaqrah & Almrs, 2022; Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022). However, those studies ignored factors related to the teachers themselves. The UTAUT model provides the main in’uential factors of technology usage behaviour, so it may be used to predict teachers’ digital teaching behaviour and students’ technology use in the fleld of education, which can provide eAective basis for improving teaching. At present, there are many extended models of UTAUT trying to enhance the explanatory power of the model (Hermita et al., 2023). However, there 

ASIA PACIFIC JOURNAL OF EDUCATION 5

has been relatively little research on the application of UTAUT at K-12 school level, especially at the elementary school level. Therefore, this study adopted the theoretical model with UTAUT as the core to explore the factors in’uencing the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers.

## _UTAUT and TPACK_

The TPACK framework was developed from Shulman’s conception of pedagogical content knowl- edge (Schulman, 1986). In order to theorize the TPACK framework, Mishra and Koehler (2006) added a third dimension related to technology knowledge (TK) to Shulman’s model, which was based on two dimensions related to pedagogical knowledge (PK) and content knowledge (CK) (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Therefore, considering the three basic dimensions (TK, PK and CK) and their interac- tion, the three overlapping dimensions logically form a seven factors model (Castéra et al., 2020): technological content knowledge (TCK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). This theore- tical framework emerged from many empirical works and practical applications (Harris et al., 2009; Koehler et al., 2007; Scott & Nimon, 2020). The TPACK framework had been used to assist teacher professional development in various subject areas (Harris & Hofer, 2011; Jimoyiannis, 2010; Kim & Bolger, 2016; Luo & Zou, 2022).

Several studies had combined TPACK with UTAUT model to explore teachers’ adoption of technology (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022; An et al., [2023)](#orcid). However, some studies have shown that the UTAUT model has some referential value in analysing technology adoption behaviours, it does not fully encompass all in’uencing factors, such as individual beliefs and the uniqueness of the teaching environment (An et al., [2023)](#orcid). Similarly, while the TPACK framework is considered an important tool for assessing the digital teaching competencies of mathematics teachers, in practice, teachers may need to adjust it according to the teaching content and the technology used (Akyuz, [2018)](#orcid). Although TPACK is regarded as a key factor in’uencing teachers’ digital teaching behaviours, research on its eAectiveness in diAerent educational settings is still insuficient (Roussinos & Jimoyiannis, 2019). Additionally, most research models did not include usage behaviour but just behavioural intention (An et al., [2023)](#orcid). For those with usage behaviour, TPACK had no signiflcant eAect on behavioural intention, but only on usage behaviour (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022). Some studies took TPACK as a total construct (Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022), while others took the speciflc dimensions of TPACK as a separate construct to aAect the dependent variable(s) (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) An et al., [2023)](#orcid). Among these research models, some of them used all seven dimensions of TPACK, and others used only four of the dimensions that were directly related to the technology. Since our study explored teachers’ use of digital technology, which focused on the technology aspect, the latter pattern was adopted in this study. TPACK was usually regarded as the important external factor in the technology acceptance model, and a signiflcant supplement to the UTAUT (An et al., [2023)](#orcid). In this study, mathematics teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) is one of the independent variables assumed to in’uence both behavioural intention and digital teaching behaviour. Some studies have already integrated TPACK into the UTAUT model. In the research by Wijaya et al., their flndings indicate that TPACK does not signiflcantly aAect usage behaviour (Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al.,  2022). However, in the study by Anthony et al., TPACK signiflcantly in’uences usage behaviour. Furthermore, the explanatory power of Anthony et al.“s research model for usage behavior has exceeded 70% (Anthony et al., [2021)](#orcid). Therefore, TPACK is a possibly important in’uencing factor. In this study, elementary school mathematics teachers” digital teaching behaviour is the dependent variable. Based on the path relationship hypotheses of the original UTAUT model, and in conjunction with the research flndings mentioned above by Wijaya et al. and Anthony et al., this study proposes the following hypotheses. The UTAUT-TPACK digital teaching behaviour conceptual model for elementary school mathematics teachers is shown in [Figure 1.](#methodology)

The following is the initial hypotheses that will be tested in this study.

**H1.** Performance expectancy aAects elementary school mathematics teachers’ behavioural inten- tion of using digital technology.

**H4.** Facilitating conditions aAect elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour.

**H5.** TPACK aAects elementary school mathematics teachers’ behavioural intention of using digital technology.

**H6.** TPACK aAects elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour.

**H7.** Behavioural intention of using digital technology aAects elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour.

# Methodology

This study used a quantitative approach to explore the in’uential factors of elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour. Six constructs, namely performance expectancy, eAort expectancy, social in’uence, facilitating conditions, behavioural intention and digital teaching behaviour in the instrument, were adopted from the UTAUT model (Venkatesh et al., 2003). TPACK was also added into the instrument as a new construct. Based on this UTAUT-TPACK model, a self- designed questionnaire was used to collect the data. It was gathered from 300 elementary school mathematics teachers in a master teacher studio. The partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) approach was used to analyse the data.

There are two parts in PLS-SEM diagnostics. Firstly, the re’ective measurement model evaluation shows indicator reliability, internal consistency reliability, convergent validity and discriminant validity of the digital teaching behaviour conceptual model for elementary school mathematics teachers. Secondly, the structural model evaluation additionally reveals the model’s overall good- ness of flt, the result of collinearity examination, the signiflcance and relevance of the structural model relationships, the coeficients of determination (R2), the eAect size (f2) and important-perfor- mance map analysis (IPMA) results.

## _Instrument and data collection_

An attempt to develop an instrument was made to explore the factors in’uencing the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers. In order to determine the feasibility of the items of the questionnaire, a number of papers were initially reviewed. Based on the items used by Venkatesh et al. (2003, 2012) and the characteristics of digital teaching, a part of the questionnaire was designed. Especially, the items of digital teaching behaviour were designed according to three dimensions (Wu & Du, 2012), namely, duration, frequency, and the number of tasks performed by using digital technology. In addition, several items designed based on the TPACK key component model (Yuan & Li, 2012) were also added into the questionnaire, and then a pilot study was conducted in a master teacher studio in Changsha on 13 May 2023. Fifty-one teachers provided valid responses. However, the discriminant validity is not satisfactory between TPACK and digital teaching behaviour (DTB). Therefore, the items of TPACK were revised according to the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Speciflcally, three items of TPACK were replaced by the following ones: “I am familiar with the illustration of various digital technology”, “I can use appro- priate digital technology to teach according to the diAerent curriculum content”, and “I know that some of the curriculum content will be replaced by other content due to the use of new digital technology”. Then, the questionnaire items were consulted with two professors and nine other researchers for the assessment of content validity. The flnal version of the questionnaire (([Table A1 ](#appendix)in the Appendix)) was obtained after being revised due to suggestions for improvement. All 30 measurement items used a 5-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree (1 point) to strongly agree (5 point). The 0–1 coding scheme was used for gender (male: 0, female: 1). The 0-1-2 coding scheme was used for professional title (junior: 0, intermediate: 1, senior: 2), and teaching experience (1–5 years: 0, 6–15 years: 1, over 15 years: 2).

The questionnaire was made by using the Wenjuanxing application ([https://www.wjx.cn)](https://www.wjx.cn). Three hundred elementary school mathematics teachers of a master teacher studio at provincial level provided valid data from 15th to 17 May of 2023. The collected data contained only a few missing values, which did not aAect the overall results, so they were directly deleted. Respondents were not required to provide their names and identities because their data was anonymous. In the ques- tionnaire, we told all the respondents that the study was voluntary and all data collected were for this study only. These hints are supposed to reduce social desirability bias (Fisher, 1993). Since almost all junior high school mathematics teachers in the state-level new area participated in this survey study, the non-response bias is supposed to have no impact on the results. We also announced that the study aimed to determine the factors aAecting the digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers.

[Table 1 ](#data-analysis)shows that 13.3% and 86.7% of the respondents are male and female, with 89.7% and 10.3% being the Han nationality and Minority nationality, respectively. There were 130 respondents with primary professional title and 141 respondents with intermediate professional title. 99.7% of respondents (299) have Bachelor’s or associate degrees. More than 80% of respondents have at least over 6 years of teaching experience. Only 18.7% of these teachers work in the rural area. [Table 1 ](#data-analysis)shows the demographics of the respondents in more detail. The average time for completing the questionnaire was 7 minutes, suggesting that these sample teachers completed the questionnaire carefully.

## _Data analysis_

The quantitative data were analysed using SPSS 26, Mplus 8.3 and SmartPLS 4. Firstly, SPSS 26 was used for data cleaning, descriptive analysis and exploratory factor analysis. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was then performed to determine the normality of the data. KMO is 0.959 indicating that the questionnaire structure is relatively good, which provides assurance for further analysis in the subsequent stages. Secondly, given that all the data comes from a single source, the presence of common method variance bias has been evaluated using Harman’s single factor test (PodsakoA et al., 2003), which tests the hypothesis that a single factor can account for all of the variance in their data. Conflrmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in Mplus 8.3 with a single factor model and a seven-factor model (performance expectancy, eAort expectancy, social in’uence, facilitating conditions, technological pedagogi- cal content knowledge, behavioural intention, and digital teaching behaviour), respectively. The fltting results showed that the seven-factor model (_X_2 = 681.719, df = 388, _X_2/df = 1.76 \< 3, RMSEA = 0.050 \< 0.08, CFI = 0.951 \> 0.9, TLI = 0.945 \> 0.9, SRMR = 0.045 \< 0.08) are much better than the single factor model (_X_2 = 2855.843, df = 405, _X_2/df = 7.05 \> 3, RMSEA = 0.142 \> 0.08, CFI = 0.588 \< 0.9, TLI = 0.558 \< 0.9, SRMR = 0.136 \> 0.08), which demonstrates that there is no pro- blem of common method variance bias. Thirdly, SmartPLS 4 was used to explore the factors in’uencing elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour. When the purpose of the study focuses on the explanation and prediction, PLS-SEM is considered to be a more suitable SEM approach than the traditional covariance-based structural equation modelling (CB-SEM) approach (J. Hair et al., 2022), which is especially true when the sample distribution is non-normal and the sample size is small. In this study, the sample data was not normal distribution and the sample size was relatively small, but it was suficient for PLS-SEM (Yuan et al., 2023a). J. Hair et al. (2022) emphasized that the two stages of PLS-SEM included measurement model evaluation and structural model evaluation. By using PLS-SEM algorithm and bootstrapping, the results of measurement model evaluation and structural model evalua- tion were obtained.

# Results

The results were divided into two parts. Firstly, the measurement model evaluation showed indicator reliability, internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity of the digital teaching behaviour conceptual model for elementary school mathematics teachers. Secondly, the structural model evaluation showed the signiflcance of the path coeficients and the coeficient of determination (R2).

## _Measurement model evaluation_

The results of reliability and validity test of this re’ective measurement model were evalu- ated ([Table 2)](#measurement-model-evaluation). Indicator loading greater than 0.708 is suitable (J. Hair et al., 2018). TPACK3 had the lowest loading at 0.790. In addition, the t-statistics of outer loadings were all greater than 2.58 at the signiflcance level of 0.01, which indicated that the measurement model had a good indicator reliability. The measurement model had a good internal consistency relia- bility when the values of Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability (CR) (UA) of all con- structs exceeded 0.7 (J. Hair et al., 2018). The lowest value of Cronbach’s alpha was owned by FC of 0.912, while that of the CR (UA) was also owned by FC of 0.914. The lowest value of average variance extracted (AVE) was owned by TPACK of 0.783, which was larger than the critical value of 0.5 (J. Hair et al., 2018). Therefore, the measurement model had a good convergent validity.

In addition, the discriminant validity was tested using the Fornell-Larcker criterion (O’Brien, 2007). The square root of AVEs should be greater than the correlation coeficient between constructs. In [Table 3,](#structural-model-evaluation) the bolded square root of AVEs on the diagonal was higher than the correlation coeficients, indicating that the measurement model had a good discriminant validity.

Fornell-Larcker criterion is better equipped with the results of calculating heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT) of correlation (J. Hair et al., 2018). The biggest HTMT value was 0.880 ([Table 4)](#structural-model-evaluation), which failed to exceed the 0.90 limit, indicating that the measurement model had an undoubted discrimi- nant validity (J. Hair et al., 2018).

So far, the indicator reliability, internal consistency reliability, convergent validity and discri- minant validity had been tested and presented, and the data were all good. This means that the measurement model evaluation was satisfactory, and the next step was the structural model evaluation.

## _Structural model evaluation_

To evaluate the structural paths by estimating the signiflcance and the size of path coeficients ()), a bootstrap (5000 samples) that produces standard errors and t-statistics to assess the statistical signiflcance of the path coeficients was executed ([Table 5)](#structural-model-evaluation).

The results showed that performance expectancy (PE) () = 0.474, _p_ \< 0.001) and TPACK () = 0.270, _p_ \< 0.001) positively in’uenced behavioural intention (BI), which conflrmed the hypotheses H1 and H4. The impact of eAort expectancy (EE) ()=-0.122, _p_ = 0.102) and social in’uence (SI) () = 0.195, _p_ = 0.058) on behavioural intention (BI) were not signiflcant. Hence, the hypotheses H2 and H3 were rejected. Likewise, TPACK () = 0.560, _p_ \< 0.001), facilitating conditions (FC) () = 0.222, _p_ \< 0.001) and behavioural intention (BI) () = 0.207, _p_ \< 0.001) positively in’uenced digital teaching behaviour (DTB). Therefore, the hypotheses H5, H6, and H7 were supported.

## _Multi-group analysis_

Multi‑group Analysis is a process used to check diAerent groups of respondents to determine if there are diAerences in the model parameters between the groups (Matthews, 2017). Partial least squares multi-group analysis (PLS-MGA) is included in the nonparametric signiflcance test in the SmartPLS 4. This study explored whether there were moderating eAects between the two groups of gender and school location and the three groups of professional title and teaching experience. The analysis steps are as follows: (1) generating data groups; (2) evaluating categorical moderator variable by bootstrap

No signiflcant diAerence was found between the two groups of school location (Table 7), professional title (intermediate vs junior) (Table 8), and three groups of teaching experience ([Table 11–13)](#multi-group-analysis). However, diAerent groups of gender had a moderating eAect on the relationship between performance expectancy (PE) and behavioural intention (BI) (diAerence\_)=-0.543, _p_ = 0.009), and the relationship between TPACK and behavioural intention (BI) (diAerence\_) = 0.389, _p_ = 0.021) (Table 6). To be speciflc, performance expectancy had a negative direct eAect on the digital teaching behaviour of female teachers () = 0.437, _p_ \< 0.001) and male teachers () = 0.980, _p_ \< 0.001). TPACK had a positive eAect on the behavioural intention of those who had more knowledge about technology. There was also a moderating eAect of professional title (senior vs junior) on “H6: facilitating conditions (FC)对digital teaching behavior (DTB)” (diAerence\_)=-0.451, _p_ = 0.03) ([Table ](#multi-group-analysis)

# Discussion

Digital technologies are the products or services supported by information technology, including digital artefacts, digital platforms, digital infrastructure, and so on. They are the tools of education digitalization and also the core of education informationization. However, elementary school mathe- matics teachers are not optimistic about their grasp of digital technology. They also have not enough time for digital teaching. Therefore, this study was intended to flnd out the main factors that aAected these teachers’ behavioural intention and actual digital teaching behaviour.

It was highlighted that TPACK had signiflcant eAects on both behavioural intention and digital teaching behaviour, and TPACK was the most in’uential factor of digital teaching behaviour. More importantly, the explanatory power of the entire model was only 58% without TPACK, but increased to 72% when TPACK was added. This was probably because TPACK component supported teachers to deliberate on what knowledge must be integrated with technology into teaching on how they can develop students’ learning (Papanikolaou et al., 2017). Therefore, the integration of technological knowledge (TK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), technological content knowledge (TCK) and TPACK employed by the teachers in teaching in’uenced their digital teaching behaviour. The result was in line with several previous studies. For example, Anthony’s study ([2021)](#orcid) showed that TPACK signiflcantly aAected digital teaching behaviour, and the explanatory power of the research model was nearly 80%. However, the result was inconsistent with other studies. For example, in Wijaya’s research model (2022), self-eficacy and TPACK were added as two new constructs in TAM model, but TPACK did not had a signiflcant in’uence on actual use of the speciflc digital technology. Moreover, in his study, the model explanatory power of digital teaching behaviour was only 47.3%, which was lower than the results of most other studies (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) An et al., [ 2023)](#orcid). The potential reason was that his study was looking at the use of microgames rather than other more pervasive digital technologies. In our study, TPACK also signiflcantly aAected behavioural intention, which was consistent with previous studies. The integration of TPACK into educational frameworks has emerged as a pivotal factor in shaping teachers’ behavioural intentions towards adopting digital technology in their teaching practices (An et al., [2023)](#orcid). The signiflcance of TPACK lies in its holistic approach to understanding how technology can be eAectively integrated with pedagogical strategies and subject matter to enhance learning 

ASIA PACIFIC JOURNAL OF EDUCATION 15

outcomes. Empirical studies have consistently demonstrated that TPACK plays a crucial role in mediating the relationship between teachers’ perceptions of performance expectancy and their intention to use digital tools in the classroom (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022). Performance expectancy, which refers to the belief that using a particular technology will improve job performance, is a key determinant of behavioural intention. When teachers possess a robust TPACK, they are more likely to perceive that digital technology will be beneflcial for their teaching, thus increasing their intention to integrate such tools. Moreover, TPACK fosters a deeper understanding of the potential synergies between technology and pedagogy, which can lead to more innovative and eAective instructional strategies. This understanding can enhance teachers’ confldence in their ability to use technology, thereby positively in’uencing their behavioural intention. The confldence stems from a clear vision of how technology can be aligned with pedagogical goals and content objectives, creating a more engaging and interactive learning environment for students. In conclusion, TPACK is not just a theoretical construct but a practical framework that signiflcantly in’uences teachers’ behavioural intentions. By recognizing and addressing the interplay between technology, pedagogy, and content, TPACK equips educators with the knowledge and skills necessary to make informed decisions about technology integration in their teaching. This, in turn, can lead to more eAective educational practices and improved student engagement and learning outcomes.

As the results showed, the most in’uential factor of teachers’ behavioural intention to use digital technology is performance expectancy. Other studies found similar results regarding the in’uence of performance expectancy on intention to use digital technology in samples from other countries (Carlsson et al., 2006; Wang & Shih, 2009; Wong et al., 2013). These studies were conducted in the context of mathematics class. This study is consistent with the results of these studies conducted in mathematics classrooms (Pittalis, 2021; Tang et al., 2023; Wijaya, Cao, Weinhandl, et al., 2022). When teachers have high performance expectancy, they believe that digital technology can help them teach better, like enhancing their teaching productivity. This suggested that if governments or schools want to promote the technology integration of mathematics teaching in elementary schools, they need to help teachers understand the usefulness of digital technology for their teaching. On the other hand, eAort expectancy did not contribute to the model signiflcantly. The results showed that when an elementary school mathematics teacher had TPACK, he or she was not aAected by the eAort expectancy any more. Some studies supported the flnding regarding the eAort expectancy (Baydas & Goktas, [2016;](#orcid) Yuen & Ma, 2002; An et al., [2023)](#orcid), while some disproved with it (Anthony et al., [2021;](#orcid) Birch & Irvine, [2009;](#orcid) Teo & Noyes, 2014; Tosuntak et al., 2014; Yuan et al.,  2023b). China had adopted corresponding policies to improve teachers’ digital competence, such as _the information technology application ability improvement project_ for elementary and secondary school teachers (MOE, 2013). Most teachers had been trained on technology, so it was not dificult for them to use most digital technologies. Therefore, the eAort expectancy was not the main factor in’uencing the behavioural intention.

Based on the results, the interesting thing was that social in’uence insigniflcantly aAected the digital teaching behaviour. This was not in line with several previous studies, which showed that social in’uence had a signiflcant eAect on teachers’ behavioural intention (Foluke, 2019). In this study, more than 80 percent of teachers had more than six years of teaching experience. They had their own understanding and ideas about the content and the use of digital technology. That was why they were not easily in’uenced by the opinions of those around them.

Facilitating conditions directly in’uenced the digital teaching behaviour. It revealed the impor- tance of technical and expert supports in the early stage of technology adoption (Geng et al., 2019). The result was consistent with previous study (Yuan et al., 2023b), which revealed that facilitating conditions was the biggest factor aAecting elementary school mathematics teachers’ usage beha- viour of dynamic mathematics software, which is a kind of subject-speciflc digital technology. Therefore, facilitating conditions tended to promote the digital teaching behaviour.

16 X. TANG ET AL.

Although our study also found that behavioural intention can positively in’uence the digital teaching behaviour of the teachers, compared with facilitating conditions and TPACK, it was less important in aAecting the digital teaching behaviour. Moreover, performance expectation was the factor that had the greatest in’uence on behavioural intention.

# Conclusions

By using the PLS-SEM approach, this study revealed factors aAecting elementary school mathe- matics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour based on a UTAUT-TPACK model. It was found that TPACK and facilitating conditions positively and signiflcantly aAected digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers, and TPACK was the biggest in’uential factor. This study contributed to improving digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers by helping government and schools to flnd out the main in’uential factors. The teachers should try their best to acquire knowledge of TPACK with the help of schools and the government in order to properly use digital technology in their classrooms. The government should enhance the training for elementary school mathematics teachers to help teachers grasp knowledge of TPACK, making them feel the usefulness of digital technology. School should provide enough hardware and software facilities, develop curriculum resources about digital teaching, and make sure elementary school mathematics teachers have experienced experts to support their digital teaching.

Based on the unifled theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTUAT), we developed a conceptual model by adding TPACK as a new construct to determine the factors that aAected elementary school mathematics teachers’ digital teaching behaviour. After adding TPACK, the explanatory power of the model increased from 58% to 72%, which proved TPACK was a very critical factor. It was deflnitely the biggest factor in’uencing digital teaching behaviour in our model. In addition, TPACK signiflcantly aAected behavioural intention and digital teaching behaviour at the same time, which was diAerent from other research models adding TPACK as a new construct as well. This is another study to add TPACK as a new construct in UTAUT model that could signiflcantly in’uence behavioural intention as well as digital teaching behaviour (Tang et al., 2023). It can also be a foundation for future study to discover more factors that aAect teachers to adopt digital technology.

TPACK is the most signiflcant factor in’uencing model has a positive and signiflcant impact on teachers’ use of digital tools. This flnding has profound implications for promoting the digital teaching practices of primary school mathematics teachers. It can assist governments and educa- tional institutions in identifying key in’uencing factors, thereby formulating eAective policies, training programmes, and digital teaching-related curriculum resources. Educators should strive to master TPACK-related knowledge to ensure the appropriate application of digital technology in the classroom. Meanwhile, schools need to provide necessary hardware and software support, develop suitable digital teaching resources, and ensure that experienced expert teams provide support to teachers in digital teaching. These measures promote teachers’ more eAective use of digital technol- ogy, thereby enhancing students’ learning achievements. If teachers do not have suficient technical knowledge, it will be dificult to carry out digital teaching. TPACK-Practical course help enhance the development of TPACK (Aktas & Ozmen, [2022)](#orcid). Developing an adaptive learning environment also improve the in-service teachers’ TPACK development (Elmaadaway & Abouelenein, 2022). Thus, we suggest that schools should have technology experts to help teachers improve their knowledge of digital technology and provide them with convenient guidance. The Chinese government had launched a project aimed at improving the ability of school mathematics teachers to use information technology since 2013, which was a long-term measure to enhance digital literacy of Chinese teachers. Elementary school mathematics teachers may be reluctant to use digital technology with a lack of facilitating conditions, therefore, hardware facilities should also be fully equipped by our government and relevant departments.

ASIA PACIFIC JOURNAL OF EDUCATION 17

TPACK is the most signiflcant factor in’uencing digital teaching behaviours, while facilitating conditions within the UTAUT model also have a notable impact on these behaviours. These flndings can be integrated into the existing theoretical frameworks of TPACK and UTAUT, underscoring the importance of integrating technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge, as well as the signiflcance of facilitating conditions in digital teaching. Given TPACK’s substantial in’uence on behavioural intentions and digital teaching behaviours, the TPACK model could be expanded to include new components such as attitudes towards digital technologies, teachers’ self-eficacy, and awareness of digital teaching resources. If research results indicate that eAort expectancy (EE) and social in’uence (SI) do not signiflcantly aAect behavioural intentions, this may challenge the importance of these components in the UTAUT model. This suggests that in digital teaching practices, teachers’ personal beliefs and technological capabilities may be more crucial than external societal expectations. Based on these flndings, the UTAUT model could be improved by adding new moderating variables, such as teachers’ digital teaching experience and familiarity with digital technologies, to better explain and predict digital teaching behaviours. This research had some limitations despite the positive results obtained. Firstly, the result from this study was from a master teacher studio which was not a random sample, thus generalizability of the results to other countries or even cities should be treated with caution. Secondly, although TPACK was added as a new construct which proved to be valid, the explanatory of research model could still be improved by adding other factors such as teacher’s belief. Finally, qualitative methods, such as in-depth interviews and even classroom observations, should be included. Further research may require a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods to explore the factors in’uencing digital teaching behaviour of elementary school mathematics teachers.
